## Development validation

This vignette accompanies development version 0.99.1.
The benchmark covers selected configurations, and the validation study uses
100 datasets per metric with 99 resampling draws. These small simulations
provide diagnostics; they do not establish general statistical calibration.
The local study observed 24% peak false positives, 10% peak detection,
74.9% transfer interval coverage, and 43% drift interval coverage in the
tested scenarios. These results limit inferential use of these methods. Report sources are `scripts/benchmark.R` and `scripts/validate.R`.

## Scope of this vignette

Electrochemical measurements (cyclic voltammetry, amperometry, impedance
spectroscopy, sensor calibration curves) share a common statistical shape:
a measured signal that contains peaks, sits on a baseline, drifts over the
course of the experiment, and must be calibrated against known concentrations
to produce a number the analyst reports. crossStatR provides four functions
for these workflows: `adaptive_baseline()` for baseline estimation,
`weighted_peak_fit()` for multi-peak fitting, `drift_correct_stat()` for
instrument drift correction with propagated uncertainty, and `robust_lod()`
for limits of detection and quantification.

This vignette works through a synthetic cyclic voltammetry example that
exhibits all four features. The example discusses the Currie (1968) and Hubaux-Vos (1970)
LOD frameworks, what drift correction does and does not do, and where the
package's defaults can mislead the analyst.

## Simulated cyclic voltammetry

The example simulates a single forward sweep from `-0.2 V` to `0.6 V` with a Gaussian
redox peak near `0.25 V`, a slowly varying quadratic baseline, additive
Gaussian measurement noise, and a linear drift in the baseline that depends
on acquisition time.

```{r sim-cv}
set.seed(202)
v <- seq(-0.2, 0.6, length.out = 400)
time_index <- seq_len(length(v))                       # seconds
baseline <- 1.0 + 0.6 * v + 0.9 * v^2                  # quadratic baseline
drift     <- 0.0008 * time_index                       # linear in time
peak1     <- 12 * exp(-(v - 0.25)^2 / (2 * 0.025^2))   # faradaic peak
noise     <- rnorm(length(v), sd = 0.08)
current   <- baseline + drift + peak1 + noise
cv_df <- data.frame(v = v, current = current, time = time_index)
```

```{r plot-cv, fig.cap = "Simulated cyclic voltammogram with a quadratic baseline, linear drift, and additive Gaussian noise. The faradaic peak sits near 0.25 V."}
ggplot(cv_df, aes(x = v, y = current)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Potential (V)", y = "Current (µA)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Baseline estimation

`adaptive_baseline()` offers two backends. The default is asymmetric least
squares (Eilers and Boelens, 2005), which iteratively reweights a penalised
least-squares fit so the baseline tracks the lower envelope of the signal.
The second backend is `lowess`, which the package includes as a sanity check rather
than as a recommended default; it does not try to be asymmetric and will
be biased upward when the signal sits well above the true baseline.

```{r baseline}
bl <- adaptive_baseline(v, current, method = "asls",
                        lambda = 1e7, p = 0.01)
print(bl)
```

Inspect the corrected signal for systematic residual structure. If the ALS
baseline tracks the top of a wide peak rather than sitting below it, the
penalty `lambda` is too small or the asymmetry parameter `p` is too large.

```{r plot-baseline, fig.cap = "Raw signal, ALS baseline, and baseline-corrected current. The corrected peak shape should be roughly symmetric and return to zero away from the peak."}
plot_df <- data.frame(
  v = rep(v, 3),
  current = c(current, bl$baseline, bl$corrected),
  what = factor(rep(c("raw", "baseline", "corrected"),
                    each = length(v)),
                levels = c("raw", "baseline", "corrected"))
)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = v, y = current, colour = what)) +
  geom_line() + facet_wrap(~ what, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Potential (V)", y = "Current (µA)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Peak fitting on the baseline-corrected signal

With the baseline subtracted the example can fit the redox peak with
`weighted_peak_fit()`. The example uses the Gaussian line shape; the Lorentzian and
pseudo-Voigt shapes are available for spectra with broader, more
non-Gaussian peaks.

```{r peakfit}
pf <- weighted_peak_fit(v, bl$corrected, peaks = "auto",
                       n_peaks = 1, peak_shape = "gaussian")
print(pf)
```

The fit returns heights, centres, and widths with `nls` asymptotic standard
errors. The example does not pick the number of peaks by AIC automatically; an extra
spurious peak in downstream analysis is usually more costly than a missed
small peak, so the example leaves the count to the analyst. Inspect `aic`, `bic`, and
the residual plot before committing to a fit.

## Drift correction with uncertainty

The linear drift in time (the `0.0008 * time_index` term) is a textbook
example of instrumental drift. In a real experiment the analyst would not know the
drift function in advance. The analyst would instead measure reference standards
periodically and pass them to `drift_correct_stat()`. Here the example simulates a
few reference readings:

```{r drift}
ref_df <- data.frame(
  time = seq(20, 380, by = 40),
  y    = 0.0008 * seq(20, 380, by = 40) + rnorm(10, sd = 0.02)
)
dri <- drift_correct_stat(current, time_index, reference = ref_df,
                          drift_model = "linear")
print(dri)
```

What drift correction does: it fits a smooth drift model to the reference
standards, anchors the corrected signal at the median reference time, and
returns a delta-method standard error on the correction at each time point.
The correction uncertainty is propagated from the drift model via the
formula `\mathrm{Var}(\hat d(t_i) - \hat d(t_{\mathrm{ref}})) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat d(t_i)) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat d(t_{\mathrm{ref}})) - 2\, \mathrm{Cov}(\hat d(t_i), \hat d(t_{\mathrm{ref}}))`.

What drift correction does *not* do: it does not make the corrected
measurements independent. If the original measurements are correlated
through shared noise structure, subtracting a fitted drift function does
not remove that correlation. Treat the corrected measurements as the analyst
would the originals for downstream independence assumptions; if the noise
has temporal autocorrelation, fit a model that accounts for it (e.g.
generalised least squares with a correlation structure, as discussed in
Davison and Hinkley, 1997, ch. 7, in the context of bootstrap resampling
for time-series data).

## Limits of detection

The example uses a separate calibration experiment for the same sensor: a
linear sweep of concentrations with measured currents.

```{r calib}
set.seed(303)
conc <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 20)
resp <- 0.5 + 2.0 * conc + rnorm(length(conc), sd = 0.25)
cal <- lm(resp ~ conc)
```

The Currie (1968) critical-value approach gives a single-point LOD based on
controlling the false-positive and false-negative rates. The classical
`3 * sigma / slope` rule corresponds to `alpha = beta = 0.00135`
(one-sided `z = 3`). The Hubaux-Vos (1970) prediction-interval approach
solves a fixed-point equation for the concentration at which the lower
prediction bound on the response at that concentration equals the upper
prediction bound at zero concentration. It is more conservative than
Currie when the calibration sample size is small because it accounts for
the calibration uncertainty itself.

```{r lod}
robust_lod(cal, method = "currie")
robust_lod(cal, method = "hubaux_vos")
```

Both methods assume the calibration is linear in the relevant range and
that the noise is approximately Gaussian. If the calibration is
nonlinear near zero, the LOD is unreliable. If the noise is
heteroscedastic, the function detects this (a lowess fit of `|r|` on `x`
whose max-to-min ratio exceeds 2) and recomputes the LOD using a local
sigma at the LOD estimate. The Monte Carlo CI on the LOD simulates from
the asymptotic distribution of `(\hat\alpha, \hat\beta, \hat\sigma)` and
recomputes the LOD for each simulation; for small calibration samples
this underestimates the true uncertainty, and the analyst should report it as a
lower bound.

The documentation does not recommend the `blank_sd` method as a default. It uses the
IUPAC `3 * sigma / slope` form with no calibration-based standard error;
use it only when the analyst has a small number of explicit blank measurements
and no usable calibration.

## What to take away

For electrochemical work: subtract the baseline with ALS, fit peaks with
`weighted_peak_fit()`, correct drift with reference standards (not the
running-median fallback), and report a Currie or Hubaux-Vos LOD with a
Monte Carlo CI. Do not claim that drift-corrected measurements are
independent; they are not. If the downstream test assumes independence
and the original noise was correlated, the drift correction will not save
the analyst.

## Measured Caltech electrochemistry data

Soedarmadji and Gregoire (2021) provide the plate 3540 electrochemistry
analysis dataset at [CaltechDATA](https://doi.org/10.25989/198p-1x22).
The packaged table contains derived diagnostics from 29 CA2 and 29 CV3
current traces. Material sample identifiers denote distinct materials;
they do not establish independent replicates of a treatment. Non-finite
current/time rows are counted explicitly before exclusion.

```{r caltech-measured-data}
caltech <- read.csv(system.file(
  "extdata", "caltech-current-summary.csv", package = "crossStatR"))
aggregate(cbind(input_rows, excluded_rows, observations) ~ analysis,
          data = caltech, FUN = sum)
head(caltech[c("analysis", "sample", "mean_photocurrent_uA",
               "slope_uA_per_s", "difference_noise_uA")])
```

The local workflow checked 348 numerical results across 58 curves and
2,975 retained observations. Means, SDs, OLS coefficients, and successive
difference SDs were compared with base R. Smoothing checks required finite
output of the expected length. These checks establish numerical agreement
for the measured inputs, rather than validation of a physical model.
The difference SD also contains genuine signal changes and is not an
independent estimate of instrumental noise.

Source processing and checks are reproducible with `scripts/validate_caltech.R`.
The test data is taken from <https://doi.org/10.25989/198p-1x22>. Attribution:
Soedarmadji, E., and Gregoire, J. (2021). *Materials Experiment and Analysis
Database: Electrochemistry analysis, Electrochemistry measurements, Material
library with V,Ca,Ar,O on plate(s) 3540*. CaltechDATA, v1.
<https://doi.org/10.25989/198p-1x22>.
